messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Kien was twenty-two, a UX designer at a startup in a city that seemed perpetually dry and orderly, which only made the memory of the flood feel more impossible. Three years earlier, during a monsoon in his native Mekong Delta, he had been trapped on a neighbor’s rooftop for fourteen hours while brown water swirled waist-deep through his house. A piece of splintered wood had struck him in the neck, leaving a dull ache that never fully faded. More viscerally, he could still taste the floodwater—a mix of mud, gasoline, and rotting fruit—as if it had just coated his tongue. Stranded alone, he had watched entire homes collapse, and when the water finally receded, he had felt a quiet certainty that he no longer belonged anywhere, that ordinary life was a stage he could only observe from behind a sheet of glass.

The causal loops began almost imperceptibly. At work, Kien would lean over his keyboard and a familiar twinge would seize his neck; in the same moment, the metallic-gritty taste would flood his mouth, and the memory would return so vividly it felt unreal. *Did it really happen?* he would wonder, but the emotion—a paralyzing helplessness—washed over him without any clear image, leaving him breathless. That disorientation fed a deeper distrust: he scanned his coworkers’ faces and concluded they were not what they seemed, that their easy laughter hid a capacity for cruelty or indifference. He had come to believe that no one else could understand what he had survived, and this isolation made him hypervigilant. As he surveyed the open-plan office for any sign of threat, the tension in his shoulders and neck tightened, reawakening the exact somatic trigger that had started the sequence. It became a self-reinforcing rhythm: neck pain conjured the taste, the taste triggered the estrangement, and the estrangement kept his body coiled, ready for disaster.

His job required collaboration, but meetings felt unbearable. When a teammate casually mentioned a coming storm, Kien’s stomach would drop and a wave of physical illness—nausea, sweating—would roll through him. That feeling of being unwell did not just cue the memory; it also confirmed his belief that he was fundamentally set apart, that others lived in a safe world he could no longer access. He started eating lunch alone in the stairwell, avoiding the break room where talk of weekend plans became another reminder of his own unspoken story. The taste would reappear even without a trigger—a sudden bitter phantom on his tongue during a presentation—and he would feel the full emotional weight of the flood, heart pounding, before any image formed. That emotion alone was enough to send him into a spiral of distrust and longing for a place that, he was certain, no longer existed for him.

By the time Kien sought help, the cycle had cost him. He had missed three deadlines, stopped attending team stand-ups, and his manager had expressed concern about his “distance.” What finally drove him to a therapist’s office was an episode in which a colleague complimented his wireframe, and instead of feeling pride, Kien felt a sudden, cold certainty that the man was lying, that no one could genuinely appreciate his work because they did not see him at all. The neck pain flared that afternoon, and the taste returned, and for a long hour he sat frozen at his desk, wondering if the memory was real or if he was losing his mind. He was most afraid of one thing: that the loop would tighten until he no longer recognized any part of his life as his own. But he was quietly hoping that someone might finally help him understand why a taste, a twinge, and a distrust of others had come to dictate everything.
